item.title: Can we tackle urban flooding without fixing how we plan our cities?
item.description:
Every monsoon, the same story unfolds: Dhaka, Chittagong, and other major cities of Bangladesh grind to a halt under the weight of severe water-logging.
But the familiar images of flooded streets conceal a far more dangerous reality -- the mixing of stormwater with overwhelmed and ageing sanitation systems.
When megacities flood, it is not just a matter of traffic disruption or inconvenience; it becomes a serious public health concern, exposing residents to contaminated water and increasing the risk of disease.
Stagnant water increases the breeding of Aedes mosquitoes, which causes dengue. It is also a matter of damaging the products, disrupting markets, and triggering cascading economic losses across industries and households.
Why does this keep happening every year?
The answer lies in how our cities have been evolving.
In a deltaic country like Bangladesh, the water system is the lifeline for the agriculture production, ecosystem and biodiversity, settlements and business centres, while river systems serve as the most efficient and reliable modes of transport.
For cities and human settlements, these water systems also functioned as natural drainage networks, allowing excess rainwater to spread, store, and gradually recede.
However, unplanned urban expansion, infrastructure and economic development the ecological value of water systems has been steadily undermined.
As a result, while water continues to define both opportunity and risk in a delta, its role in shaping where and how our cities expand has been largely overlooked.
Natural drainage pathways have been disrupted, retention areas diminished, and urban development has expanded into locations that are inherently vulnerable to flooding.
The outcome is a system that struggles to cope even with seasonal rainfall, making flooding not an exception, but an annual certainty.
More intense rainfall events and rising river levels linked to climate change are increasing the frequency and severity of flooding.
In short, big cities flooding is not just about heavy rain -- it’s also a result of how the city has grown and managed its infrastructure.
Improving drainage, protecting wetlands, and better urban planning are key to reducing the problem.
Is t ackling urban flooding a political p riority?
One of the top political commitments of the BNP’s election manifesto (2026) was restoring and protecting Bangladesh’s natural water systems as part of its broader environmental and economic strategy.
In practical terms, this includes 20,000km c anal ( khal ) re-excavation and restoration to revive natural drainage and navigation systems, protection of rivers, canals, wetlands, and other waterbodies from encroachment and illegal filling, ensuring free flow of water by removing blockages and restoring connectivity between waterways, and strengthening regulation and enforcement to prevent future degradation of water systems.
This clarifies that tackling u rban f looding is one of the top priorities of the current government.
The next question is how these political manifestos could be translated into development actions?
Is urban flooding only an engineeri ng concern?
At present, much of our response to urban flooding remains centred on engineering solutions. Drains are widened, pumps are installed, and embankments are constructed.
These interventions are necessary, but they often address symptoms rather than causes.
Flooding in our cities is not simply the result of inadequate drainage; it is also the outcome of how land has been used and misused over time.
Canals have been filled, wetlands encroached upon, and natural retention areas converted into built-up areas.
In effect, we have reduced the very spaces that once allowed cities to absorb and manage water.
Improper waste disposal is one of the reasons for clogging drainages while sanitation adds another layer to this challenge.
In many parts of our cities, sewerage systems will not be enough if they are not linked to drainage and land-use planning. Globally, cities facing similar challenges are beginning to adopt more adaptive planning approaches.
This planning process facilitates flexible options to living with water through increasing the capacity to absorb, store, and gradually release rainwater through green spaces, permeable surfaces, and restored water bodies.
Integrating this logic into modern urban planning could help reduce flood risks while improving overall urban livability.
Can this be managed sustainably?
The economic transformation of Bangladesh will lead to an increased rate of urbanization, and the pressure on cities will only intensify.
More people, more buildings, and more infrastructure will compete for the same limited space. In a delta, this makes the question of location unavoidable, and spatial planning becomes critical.
Where we allow development, how we regulate density, and whether we preserve natural water systems all determine how cities respond to rainfall.
Without integrating these spatial considerations into policy decisions, investments in drainage and sanitation will continue to fall short of expectations.
Equally important is the need to shift from short-term, project-based thinking to long-term, system-based planning.
The Delta Plan 2100 provides a useful framework in this regard, but its success will depend on instrumenting the Spatial Planning Framework, a three-tier planning from the National, Regional, and Local level Spatial Planning, following a strong institutional framework to guide and regulate rational land use practices and to synchronize all the development actions.
How can we turn this challenge into an opportunity?
If we are serious about addressing urban flooding and sanitation, we also need to rethink how these sectors are financed and delivered.
Historically, these have been considered as public works functions and dependent on government budgets and implemented through projectized approaches.
But in reality, these are also service sectors with economic value , and they offer untapped opportunities for private investments.
The challenge is not the absence of capital, but the absence of bankable, well-structured models and institutional readiness to attract the private sector investors from home and abroad.
Drainage and sanitation projects are often too narrowly defined, focused on isolated engineering solutions, and disconnected from land use and urban development.
As a result, potential investors see high risks but limited returns. This is where a more integrated approach can make a difference.
If urban water management is planned aligning with the concepts of integrated land use, infrastructure, real estate development, new possibilities begin to emerge.
Protecting flood flow zones and improving drainage, for instance, can significantly increase land values in surrounding areas.
With the right policy framework, a portion of that value can be captured to finance infrastructures.
Similarly, wastewater treatment and reuse can evolve into service-based business models, supplying water to industry or supporting circular economy initiatives.
Ultimately, the goal is not to privatize urban services, but to mobilize all available resources from both public and private sources towards a common public good.
If we can combine sound spatial planning with innovative financing and effective governance, the challenge of urban flooding and sanitation can be transformed into an opportunity for building more resilient, healthier, and better-suited to the realities of living in a delta.
How can we sustain our actions?
Beyond integrated urban planning, engineering and political will, effective communication serves as the vital link that turns policy into public action and contributes to sustaining the resilience.
In the context of Bangladesh’s urban flooding, communication is not merely about broadcasting weather forecasts; it should connect data with community behaviour.
How can we better educate our citizens that while city floods, we suffer altogether, it damages everyone’s property and affects everyone despite which economic class we belong to or where we live Baridhara or Gulshan or in Korail.
The effective communication can play a powerful role in influencing citizen’s behaviour -- helping citizens in cities like Dhaka understand how encroaching wetlands or blocking drains leads to flooding.
Combined with public education, a sense of ownership among common citizens, and strong institutions and governance, communication can shift the narrative from passive victimhood to collective stewardship.
This alignment is critical to sustaining initiatives under the Bangladesh Delta Plan 2100, ensuring resilience is not just planned, but practised.
Achieving these demands, re-designing institutions, would be essential to ensure the livability of ourselves, for our next generation, and the generations to come.
Shaikh Muhammad Mehedi Ahsan is the Principal Coordinator, Spatial Planning Affairs, and Vice President (01) of the Bangladesh Institute of Planners (BIP), working on urban resilience and infrastructure planning.

item.title: Zubaida Rahman stresses women’s empowerment for social progress
item.description:
Prime Minister’s wife Dr Zubaida Rahman on Monday underscored the importance of women’s empowerment, saying women can play a vital role in family welfare, healthcare and rural development.
“If everyone contributes from their respective positions toward building the desired society, it would certainly be possible to achieve that goal,” she said while addressing the annual gathering and fair organised by Bangladesh Police Women Welfare Association (PUNAK) as the chief guest.
She also stressed the importance of ensuring the safety and development of girl children. “Every girl should be able to pursue the future she dreams of and the state system should support that path instead of creating obstacles,” she said.
At the outset of her speech, Dr Zubaida, also a cardiologist, paid tribute to BNP founder and former president Ziaur Rahman and former prime minister Khaleda Zia.
“First of all, I respectfully remember martyred president Ziaur Rahman and former prime minister Khaleda Zia. I am very pleased to be present at this event organised by PUNAK today. I congratulate all members for their tireless efforts and contributions to different levels of society,” she said.
She said the activities carried out by PUNAK members are helping guide future generations toward contributing positively to society.
“The social welfare initiatives you have undertaken for past, present and future development collectively lay the foundation for a beautiful, healthy and humane society,” she added.
She also called for encouraging women entrepreneurs in small, cottage and medium industries on the basis of merit through training, development and marketing support.
She said such initiatives would help increase family solvency, ensure children’s education and facilitate poverty alleviation.
She thanked all members of PUNAK for organising the event.
Spouse of Home Minister Hasina Ahmed and Cultural Affairs Secretary Kaniz Mowla , among other, attended the programme as guests of honour.
Leaders and members of the PUNAK family were also present at the event.

item.title: Disability inclusion in focus at pre-budget meeting with finance minister
item.description:
Representatives of persons with disabilities on Sunday urged the government to ensure stronger budgetary allocation and policy support for disability inclusion in the upcoming national budget for the 2026–27 fiscal year.
The call came during a pre-budget consultation meeting held at the Finance Division conference room at the Bangladesh Secretariat, where leaders of disability rights organizations met with Finance Minister Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury to discuss the rights, welfare, and inclusion of persons with disabilities in national development planning.
The meeting, held at 3:30pm on Sunday, was also attended by Social Welfare Minister AZM Zahid Hossain and State Minister for Social Welfare Farzana Sharmin.
Speaking at the meeting, Finance Minister Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury said the government remains committed to ensuring the rights and welfare of persons with disabilities.
“This government is disability-friendly. We are giving the highest importance to issues concerning persons with disabilities,” he said.
The finance minister also stressed the importance of moving beyond a charity-based approach toward empowerment and self-reliance.
“We do not want to see persons with disabilities only through a charity model. We need to work more so that they can become self-reliant. Only providing allowances will not improve their quality of life,” he said.
He also said that each ministry would appoint a focal person on disability affairs to strengthen coordination and inclusion across government institutions.
Social Welfare Minister AZM Zahid Hossain said the government has clear directives from Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to ensure equal opportunities and facilities for persons with disabilities.
“There are special instructions from the prime minister so that persons with disabilities receive all necessary opportunities and services,” he said.
State Minister for Social Welfare Farzana Sharmin said the government had already started working on several proposals raised during the consultation.
“The government has already initiated work on the proposals that have been submitted,” she said.
“We may not be able to fulfil all demands within a short time, but we will gradually work to ensure that ministry-based budgets properly allocate funds considering the needs of persons with disabilities,” the state minister added.
A 23-member delegation from Bangladesh Protibondhi Kallyan Somity (BPKS) and the National Alliance of Disabled People's Organizations (NADPO) took part in the discussion.
The delegation was led by Md Abdus Sattar Dulal, founder and executive director of BPKS and president of NADPO.
According to participants, the discussion focused on ensuring meaningful participation of persons with disabilities in mainstream development activities and incorporating disability-inclusive measures into the national budget.
Representatives also emphasized the need for specific allocations, accessible public services, and policy-level commitments to improve the socio-economic condition of persons with disabilities across the country.
Among others present at the meeting were former government secretary and BPKS Adviser Abi Abdullah, NADPO Secretary General Md Iftekhar Hossain Sohel, and disability representatives from different districts.
The consultation was part of a series of pre-budget discussions organized by the Finance Division ahead of the formulation of the national budget for the 2026–27 fiscal year.

item.title: Arsenal glimpse title glory as VAR 'earthquake' rocks EPL
item.description:
Arsenal are within touching distance of their first Premier League crown for 22 years after a VAR "earthquake" rocked the title race in their contentious 1-0 win at West Ham on Sunday.
Mikel Arteta's side were embroiled in a controversial stoppage-time incident that looked set to derail their title bid before a VAR intervention tilted the balance of power back to north London.
Leading through Leandro Trossard's deflected 83rd minute goal, the Gunners were stunned when West Ham's Callum Wilson lashed home in the final moments after Arsenal keeper David Raya dropped the ball inside his penalty area.
But West Ham's celebrations were curtailed when VAR official Darren England told referee Chris Kavanagh to consult the pitch-side monitor to check a potential foul by Pablo on Raya before his fumble.
After a lengthy delay ratcheted up the drama, Kavanagh agreed that Pablo had impeded the keeper and returned to the pitch to announce the goal had been disallowed.
Arteta and his players breathed a collective sigh of relief, while Arsenal's fans exploded in celebration as jeers rang out from disbelieving West Ham supporters.
It was a moment of such emotional intensity that it will surely stand as the defining image of the season if Arsenal go on to win their 14th English title and first since 2004.
The Gunners are five points clear of second-placed Manchester City and will be crowned champions if they win their last two matches at home to Burnley on May 18 and at Crystal Palace on May 24.
They could seal the trophy even earlier if City fail to win their game in hand against Palace at the Etihad Stadium on Wednesday.
That would allow Arsenal to wrap up the title with a victory over relegated Burnley.
For third-bottom West Ham, it was a brutal blow in their battle to avoid relegation.
The Hammers remain one point from safety but fourth-bottom Tottenham would extend that gap to four with just two games left if they beat Leeds on Monday.
'Doubt and speculation' What was surely the most consequential VAR decision in Premier League history inevitably sparked differing verdicts from Arteta and West Ham boss Nuno Espirito Santo.
"It was a call from the ref that is very brave," Arteta said. "I have to praise them, for giving the option to a referee to decide, away from the lights and the chaos, to give clarity to him to make the right call.
"When you look at the action in that way, it is an obvious error. It is a free-kick, and the goal has to be disallowed.
"You're talking about a moment that can decide the history, and the course, of two massive clubs that are fighting with their lives to achieve their objectives.
"The pressure is huge. So congratulations, because they made a big call in very difficult circumstances."
Nuno saw it far differently, insisting the decision was the result of debatable rule-making and inconsistent interpretation of those laws in recent seasons.
"The way the game finished, we're all upset of course," he said.
"There's a referee, there's VAR, there's circumstances in the past that would be judged different.
"Even the referees don't know what is a foul, what isn't a foul. It creates a lot of doubt and speculation around it."
Since being introduced to the Premier League in 2019, VAR has been a lightning rod for criticism from managers and fans infuriated by a system that is far from fool-proof and often sucks the spontaneity out of matches.
But former Manchester United and England defender Gary Neville felt the seismic call was correct: "This is an earthquake, a tremor of a moment.
"It is probably the biggest moment in VAR history in the Premier League. This is massive.
"I think it's a foul. His arm is held on Raya. It's on him all the time. He's holding across his neck and chest."
Whether the decision was legitimate or not, the after-shocks will be felt from London all the way to Manchester.
